guard: the foreign-slot orphan predicate reclaims ONLY a slot whose holder's gate has provably reopened past its stamp, and refuses every other observation
why: The defect (#1393) was a branch that refused unconditionally where the same function's own-instance branch two lines below already reclaimed on identical evidence, so the fix is a predicate and the predicate is what has to be graded. The rows below split into two halves that must red on DIFFERENT cells, because a fixture that only proved the reclaim path would be graded half the change. Rows 1-2 sever the RECOVERY: the predicate stops admitting the orphan, and the operator's state is unrecoverable again. Rows 3-7 sever the GUARD, and those are the rows that matter more: a fix for an unrecoverable state that quietly makes a live slot stealable would be a worse defect than the one it closed. Row 8 severs the seam's own optionality. Row 9 severs the BINDING carry-forward, and it is the row a reviewer had to find rather than the fixture: the suite passed that mutant green because the staged descriptor declared no governed trait, so the binding map was empty and every cell about it compared `{}` to `{}`. Every row edits code, never a comment, and the completion marker is the suite's final banner, which it prints on either outcome, so a run that dies before the graded cell reports INCONCLUSIVE rather than passing as a kill. Each row carries a core build in its `command` and an `afterRestore` that rebuilds: the suite lives under implementations/ and imports @cotal-ai/core, which resolves to dist/, so a mutation to packages/core/src that did not rebuild would be read by nothing and report a false SURVIVED. dist/ is gitignored, so the rebuild after restore is the only thing that stops the tree keeping a build compiled from the mutant.

mutations.name: RECOVERY SEVERED at the comparison: the in-flight arm swallows the orphan case
mutations.find:
if (observed === slot.generation)
    throw new EpEnvelopeError("conflict", `${held}; its issuance gate is still at generation ${slot.generation}
mutations.replace:
if (observed >= slot.generation)
    throw new EpEnvelopeError("conflict", `${held}; its issuance gate is still at generation ${slot.generation}
mutations.expectRed: B REGISTERS - the state the operator could not exit is now exited by B's ordinary start
mutations.cell: B REGISTERS - the state the operator could not exit is now exited by B's ordinary start
mutations.note: The OFF-BY-ONE mirror of the row named `the in-flight equality arm can never fire`, and the reason both exist: both edit the same equality arm, in opposite directions. Widening it from `===` to `>=` swallows the orphan case, which fails SAFE and is therefore the easy one to ship by accident: nothing becomes stealable, the operator is simply stuck again. Narrowing the same arm to `<` makes it unreachable and is the dangerous one. A fixture carrying only one would leave the opposite off-by-one ungraded. An earlier draft wrote `<=` here, which is the SAME predicate as the shipped `===` once the `observed < slot.generation` arm above has already returned, so it changed no behaviour and mutation-proof correctly reported SURVIVED. That is the equivalent-mutant trap this note exists to record: on a chain of ordered arms, the direction that matters is the one the preceding arms have not already excluded.

mutations.name: RECOVERY SEVERED at the call site: the predicate is never consulted for a foreign slot
mutations.find:
} else if (gov.provisional.instanceId !== args.instanceId)
        await assertForeignSlotIsOrphaned(gov.provisional, spec.endpoint, args.observeHolderGeneration);
mutations.replace:
} else if (gov.provisional.instanceId !== args.instanceId)
        throw new EpEnvelopeError("conflict", `a concurrent registration for endpoint "${spec.endpoint}" (instance "${gov.provisional.instanceId}") holds the governance slot through its spec publication; re-read and re-decide (SPEC 13.7/13.8)`);
mutations.expectRed: B REGISTERS - the state the operator could not exit is now exited by B's ordinary start
mutations.cell: B REGISTERS - the state the operator could not exit is now exited by B's ordinary start
mutations.note: This is the pre-fix behaviour verbatim: the foreign branch refuses unconditionally and the predicate is never consulted, which is exactly the code #1393 reports. It severs the WIRING rather than the predicate's body, and the two are distinguishable only by mutating each separately: a predicate that is correct and never called is the same defect with a better-looking diff. It is aimed at the call site rather than at the seam guard inside the predicate because a mutant that throws before `observeHolderGeneration` is read leaves that parameter unused and `observed` unnarrowed, and the core build then fails TS2722/TS18046 before the suite runs at all; a compile error is not a red, and mutation-proof correctly grades it WRONG-RED rather than a kill.

mutations.name: GUARD SEVERED: `<` widened to `<=`, so the in-flight refusal answers the WRONG code and the wrong reason
mutations.find:
if (observed < slot.generation)
    throw new EpEnvelopeError("unavailable", `${held} at generation ${slot.generation}, ahead of its observed live gate generation ${observed}
mutations.replace:
if (observed <= slot.generation)
    throw new EpEnvelopeError("unavailable", `${held} at generation ${slot.generation}, ahead of its observed live gate generation ${observed}
mutations.expectRed: B REFUSES while A's registration is genuinely in flight - a live slot is never stolen
mutations.cell: B REFUSES while A's registration is genuinely in flight - a live slot is never stolen
mutations.note: WHAT THIS ROW ACTUALLY GRADES, stated precisely because an earlier draft of this note overclaimed it. Widening `<` to `<=` does NOT make a live slot stealable: the equal-generation case still REFUSES, it is just refused one arm earlier, so the answer moves from `conflict` ("IN FLIGHT, wait, here is the remedy") to `unavailable` ("ahead or garbled observation"). What it severs is the refusal's CLASS and its reason, and both are load-bearing: `conflict` is what tells a caller to re-read and re-decide, and the message is what names `cotal reconcile-gate` as the exit. Measured first-hand rather than predicted: an earlier draft named the MESSAGE cell as the first red, on the reasoning that only the wording would move. Running the mutant showed the refusal cell itself reds first, because it asserts `code === "conflict"` and the ahead-of-us arm answers `unavailable`. A cell testing only `didThrow` would stay green through this mutant, which is why the control asserts the code and the wording rather than the mere fact of a refusal. The genuinely permissive off-by-one at this coordinate is the row below, which is the one that makes an in-flight slot stealable.

mutations.name: GUARD SEVERED: the in-flight equality arm can never fire, so a LIVE in-flight slot is stealable
mutations.find:
if (observed === slot.generation)
    throw new EpEnvelopeError("conflict", `${held}; its issuance gate is still at generation ${slot.generation}
mutations.replace:
if (observed < slot.generation)
    throw new EpEnvelopeError("conflict", `${held}; its issuance gate is still at generation ${slot.generation}
mutations.expectRed: B REFUSES while A's registration is genuinely in flight - a live slot is never stolen
mutations.cell: B REFUSES while A's registration is genuinely in flight - a live slot is never stolen
mutations.note: THE ROW THE WHOLE FIXTURE EXISTS FOR: the mutation that actually trades an unrecoverable state for a stealable one. The arm above has already thrown for every `observed < slot.generation`, so rewriting this arm's test to `<` makes it UNREACHABLE. The equal case then falls off the end of the predicate, which is its success path, and the slot-take replaces a slot whose holder is mid-publish. It is the mirror of row 1: same line, and widening in the direction the preceding arms have NOT excluded fails DANGEROUS where row 1's widening fails safe. It reds on the refusal cell, which asserts a throw at all, so no wording assertion is doing the work here.

mutations.name: GUARD SEVERED: a throwing observation is treated as absence rather than a refusal
mutations.expectRed: the observation THROWS -> `unavailable`; unreadable is not absent
mutations.cell: the observation THROWS -> `unavailable`; unreadable is not absent
mutations.note: AGENTS.md forbids a fallback, and this is the fallback shape that looks most reasonable in a diff: an unreadable gate becomes `assume it is old`, which reclaims a slot whose holder may be mid-publish. It reds on its own cell rather than on the reclaim cells, because a mutant that admits MORE leaves every positive path green.

mutations.name: GUARD SEVERED: a garbled observation is coerced to a number instead of refused
mutations.find:
if (!wireInt(observed))
    throw new EpEnvelopeError("unavailable", `${held}, and its issuance-gate generation could not be observed; refusing rather than racing a registration that may still be in flight (SPEC 13.7): observed ${JSON.stringify(observed)}, not an unsigned generation`);
mutations.expectRed: a non-integer observation -> `unavailable`; a garbled generation is never coerced
mutations.cell: a non-integer observation -> `unavailable`; a garbled generation is never coerced
mutations.note: The seam is injected, so its return value is caller-supplied and is validated rather than trusted, exactly as `deregisterServiceInstance` validates its own `observeGeneration`. `Number("7")` is 7, so this mutant makes a string observation decide an authority question. It coerces INSIDE the refusal arm and still refuses what will not coerce, which keeps `observed` narrowed for the comparisons below: a replacement that dropped the refusal outright left the value `unknown` and failed the core build on TS18046 before the suite ran, which mutation-proof grades WRONG-RED rather than as a kill.

mutations.name: GUARD SEVERED: the ahead-of-us refusal is dropped, so a stale read licenses a reclaim
mutations.find:
if (observed < slot.generation)
    throw new EpEnvelopeError("unavailable", `${held} at generation ${slot.generation}, ahead of its observed live gate generation ${observed}; refusing rather than treating an ahead or garbled observation as an abandoned slot (SPEC 13.7)`);
mutations.expectRed: an observation BEHIND the slot's stamp -> `unavailable`; ahead-or-garbled never licenses a reclaim
mutations.cell: an observation BEHIND the slot's stamp -> `unavailable`; ahead-or-garbled never licenses a reclaim
mutations.note: Deleting this arm does not make the slot reclaimable on its own (the equality arm below still refuses the equal case), so what it actually admits is the strictly-behind case: an observation that is stale or garbled in the one direction no shipped path can produce. `deregisterServiceInstance` refuses the same coordinate for the same reason, and this row is what keeps the two seams agreeing.

mutations.name: SEAM OPTIONALITY SEVERED: an absent seam silently reclaims instead of refusing
mutations.find:
if (typeof observeHolderGeneration !== "function")
    throw new EpEnvelopeError("conflict", `${held}; re-read and re-decide. This registration cannot observe that instance's issuance gate, so it cannot tell an in-flight registration from an abandoned one and refuses (SPEC 13.7/13.8)`);
mutations.expectRed: NO SEAM wired -> refuses exactly as today, so no caller silently gains a reclaim it never asked for
mutations.cell: NO SEAM wired -> refuses exactly as today, so no caller silently gains a reclaim it never asked for
mutations.note: The seam is OPTIONAL, so its absent case is a real branch with real callers: every registration path that has not wired it keeps today's refusal. This mutant turns absence into blanket permission, which would hand a reclaim to callers that never asked for one and can prove nothing about the holder. It is the row that makes the optionality safe rather than merely convenient.

mutations.name: BINDING LAUNDERED: the slot-take drops the endpoint's binding impositions
mutations.expectRed: a slot-take carries the BINDING forward: C's committed-but-unacked take left it intact, not laundered
mutations.cell: a slot-take carries the BINDING forward: C's committed-but-unacked take left it intact, not laundered
mutations.note: THE ROW THAT CLOSES A VACUOUS PROOF, and it exists because the suite once passed this exact mutant 30/30 green. A reclaim replaces `provisional` and must carry `commands` (the BINDING impositions) forward untouched; dropping them launders a published surface's obligations away, which is a worse outcome than the defect #1393 reports. Two things had to change before this row could grade anything. First, the staged descriptor carried NO governed trait, so `readGovernedDeclarations` recorded nothing, `serializeGovernanceCommands` dropped the empty set, and the binding map was `{}` for the whole suite: section 7 compared `{}` to `{}` and passed whatever the reclaim did. The descriptor now declares `ai.cotal.guarded` and the cells assert the map's CONTENTS. Second, the cell had to observe the right coordinate: a COMPLETED registration ends in `promoteHeldGovernance`, which merges the binding with the registrant's own provisional declarations, so a successor re-declaring the same commands rebuilds an identical map and hides the drop. Section 6's residue is where it is visible - C's slot-take COMMITTED and its ack was lost, so the head holds exactly what the slot-take wrote with nothing promoted over it. Measured, not predicted: this mutant reds on that one cell and no other.
